setup.zh: 正殿里没有神像，只有一口空的石座，四方，四足。石座前立着测灵石，观主玄沉子坐在一旁。轮到你了。
setup.en: No statue in the main hall — only an empty stone seat, square, on four feet. Before it stands the spirit stone; the abbot Xuanchenzi sits beside it. It is your turn.

recap.zh: 测灵石测出了你的灵根；瞿老说「腿稳，心细」，观主说：收，外门。
recap.en: The spirit stone read your roots; Elder Qu said "steady legs, careful heart," and the abbot said: take them — the outer court.

zh: 正殿没有神像，只有一口空的石座。
四方，四足，大得能躺下一个人。
测灵石前，把手放上去——看它亮几种颜色。
en: No statue in the hall — only an empty stone seat.
Square, four-footed, big enough to lie in.
Before the spirit stone: lay your hand on it, and see how many colours it shows.

text.zh: 石面正中一块颜色比别处深，四四方方，仿佛许多年前，那上头曾经压过一样很重很重的东西。
text.en: In the middle of the stone top is a patch darker than the rest, square, as if many years ago something very, very heavy had once pressed down on it.

text.zh: 石面光溜溜的，正中凹下去一块，是千百只手按出来的。你把手心在衣襟上擦了两擦。
text.en: The stone is worn smooth, a hollow pressed into its middle by a thousand hands. You wipe your palm twice on your coat.

text.zh: 那扫地的老头不知什么时候也进了殿，拄着扫帚，靠在门框上，谁也不看。
text.en: Somehow the old sweeper has come into the hall too; he leans on his broom against the doorframe and looks at no one.

story.zh:
正殿在山门里头最高的一层台子上。殿很大，很旧，梁上的彩画褪得只剩了影子，殿里没有神像，只在正中间，摆着一口空的石座。那石座四四方方，底下四只脚，大得能躺下一个人，石面正中一块颜色比别处深，四四方方，仿佛许多年前，那上头曾经压过一样很重很重的东西。石座前头，立着一块一人多高的测灵石，灰不溜秋，看不出什么稀奇。石座旁边一张蒲团上，坐着观主——早上鼋背上那个人。一身灰袍，面目温和，看上去比山下镇上卖布的掌柜还要和气几分；可殿里一百来个孩子，没有一个敢抬头多看他一眼。那扫地的老头不知什么时候也进了殿，拄着扫帚，靠在门框上。

过了三试的孩子，统共一百来个，在殿里排成长长的一队。小满排在最后，只马小宝一个是滑竿抬上来的，排在他后头。唱名的，还是早上石阶底下那个执事，靠在柱子上。

有孩子问这石座是做什么的，为什么不供神仙，唱名执事道：「给鼎留的。三百年了。」

执事拿下巴指一指测灵石，打了个呵欠，照例背规矩——三年背一回，背得像念经：「手按上去。金白，木青，水黑，火红，土黄，身上有哪样，亮哪样。亮一种的，叫单灵根，也叫天灵根——上上。」又一个呵欠，「别瞅了，本观三百年，没测出过一个。天灵根的娃娃，襁褓里就叫大宗门拿银子抱走了，轮不着上这儿爬台阶。山门外头，人家先挑；挑剩下的进了山门，才是本观的。」一个孩子问：「襁褓里的娃娃，话都不会说，怎么看得出来？」执事眼皮也不抬：「《抱朴子》上写着：『诸得仙者，皆其受命偶值神仙之气，自然所禀。故胞胎之中，已含通道之性。』娘胎里带来的，石头不过照一照。」

殿里没有人笑这一句。小满看着那张没睡醒的脸。他想起码头上那一片青，想起那一声「哥——」。娘胎里带来的，石头照一照，银子一放，人便抱走了。原来这是规矩，规矩还写在书上。

执事接着背，越背越快：「两种，双灵根，上中；三种，三灵根，中上——都算真灵根。四种、五种，伪灵根：四种，下中；五种全亮的——」他拖长了声音，眼皮撩起来，在队伍里溜了一圈，「下下。颜色越少越亮，越好。不亮颜色，起风、打闪、结霜的，叫异灵根，本观没见过，你们也甭想。今年外门收一百零八个，玄沉子观主点头，便是收。」他提着笔，在名册上一个一个地数，收一个，划一笔。数到中间，笔尖在一行上滑了过去，没停，那一行底下是四个新写的字。

队伍一寸一寸地往前挪。前头每亮一回石头，殿里便响一回——那光不是浮在石面上的，是从石头肚里一层一层透出来，透一回，满殿便凉一分，像刚下过一场雨——亮得好的，一片惊叹；亮得暗的，一片笑。昨夜廊下那个光脚的孩子排在前头，脚底板上的草叶子还没摘，一按，亮了四种颜色，「下中」。他咧开嘴，回头冲人堆里竖起一根指头。执事照例问生辰，他张口报了一个年份——石阶底下他报的是十二——报完了，脸一下子白了。执事掐着指头一算：「十一。告示上写的，十二起。」那孩子道：「过了年就十二！」执事道：「过了年，再过三年，下回开山门，你再来。」观主看了他一会儿，没有点头。那孩子没哭，走到殿角，攥着他那块三道画满的考牌，站着。

殿两侧另摆着一溜蒲团，坐着五六个人，也是灰袍，却一个比一个静，静得像殿里的柱子——那是本观的长老，平日在后山闭关，三年里也就这一天肯下来。石头亮得浑的，他们眼皮也不抬；亮得清爽的，才有人把茶盏放下。方才一个双灵根的孩子，金、水两色，清清爽爽，手一拿开，左手头一位赭袍的长老便开了口：「这个，记在我名下。」那孩子愣了半天，才被人推着，到蒲团跟前磕了头。这叫挑徒弟：长老看中谁，当场开口，观主不拦；被挑中的叫记名弟子，名字写在长老名下，人先在外门待着，等筑了基，才搬去长老的洞府。

小满一面挪，一面数：前头还有三十一个人，名册上还剩三十二个名额——够，连他，刚刚够。挪到前头剩二十个的时候，身后一挤，马家的家丁把马小宝塞到了他前头。小满又数了一遍：前头二十一个，名额二十一个。他自己，是第二十二个。孙二狗排在小满前头不远，回过头来冲他咧了咧嘴，小声道：「三步一口气。」二试他是把五搁在了中间，「因为五在一到九的正当中，跟饭碗搁在桌子正当中一个道理」，老执事听了半天，说道理不对，意思对了，给他画了一道；三试他是闭着眼睛冲进去的，冲到古松底下，一头撞在树上，撞出一个包，算是摸过了。

轮到孙二狗了。他把手放上去，测灵石半天没有动静，好一会儿，才极勉强地透出一点光来，四种颜色，淡得像隔着一层窗户纸。唱名的执事还当是石头坏了，伸手在石头上拍了两下，那光也不见亮。执事叹了口气，念道：「金、木、火、土，四门，伪灵根，色又极淡。下下之资。」殿里有人笑。孙二狗没有笑，也没有低头，只把那个比他身子还大的包袱，往背上紧了紧。那包袱里装的，是他娘给他缝的三双鞋，一双比一双大，是预备着他在山上一年一年地长个子的。观主看了他一会儿，点了点头。执事划了一笔。

排在小满前面第三个的，是阿禾。她把两根小辫子往肩后一甩，走到测灵石跟前，却没急着按，先低头看了看自己的手——手背上一道一道的皴口子，是守了一秋天白菜守出来的——在袍子上擦了两擦，这才按了上去。

测灵石亮了。只亮了一种颜色。

是青。起先只是石头肚里一点，像开春头一天，冻土底下顶出来的一粒芽尖；跟着那一点往外涨，涨满了一块石头，又从石头里涨出来，涨满了一座殿。那青不浑，不杂，干干净净，一丝别的颜色也没有，亮得满殿的人一齐抬起胳膊挡眼睛，挡了还是亮，从指头缝里钻进来，钻得眼皮底下都是绿的。殿里那股凉意，一下子换成了另一股味儿：新翻的泥土，掐断的青草汁子，像有人在这座三百年没供过神的殿里，一夜种下了一亩地。

码头上那一片青，小满早上见过。那是鸡蛋大的一块石头。

殿里没有一点声音。侧座上那五六位长老，不知什么时候都睁开了眼。唱名的执事嘴还半张着——「本观三百年，没测出过一个」，这句话才背完不到一炷香，还挂在他嘴边上，没来得及收，叫这一片青，一巴掌扇了回去。他那双没睡醒的眼睛，这一回是真醒了，醒得发直。可他头一个动作不是念，是扭过脸去，往殿门外头瞟了一眼。

殿门外头什么也没有，只有日头，和靠在门框上的那个扫地老头。小满却知道他在瞟谁：天不亮的时候，码头上，一个穿白的抱走了一个亮青的娃，上车之前，冲这个人点过一点头。

执事张了张嘴：「木……木——」

一个「天」字还没出口，蒲团上那个人站了起来。一百来个孩子测了大半天，玄沉子没挪过一挪，亮得好，他点头，亮得暗，他也点头，像庙里一尊会点头的泥像。这时候他站起来了，从石座边上走下来，不快，灰袍的下摆拂过青砖，一点声音也没有。他走到阿禾跟前，那一片青还没散，把他一张和气的脸也照青了。他伸出一只手，按在阿禾头顶上，按在两根黄毛小辫子当中，道：

「这个，我收了。」

侧座上有位白眉毛的长老，已经欠起了半个身子，听了这一句，又慢慢坐了回去。

观主说完，顺着执事方才那一眼，朝殿门外头望过去，声音不高，不像是说给殿里的人听的：

「沉鼎观的人。」

门框上的扫地老头，扫帚在门槛上「笃」地一顿。执事的笔悬在名册上，半天落不下去，末了在那一行底下写了两个字：亲传。字比平常写得小。写完了，照旧在名额上划了一笔。小满跟着又数了一遍：他还是第二十二个。

殿里这才「轰」的一声炸开了。有人掰着指头数那「三百年」，有人踮着脚往前挤，想瞧瞧那丫头长了几只眼睛；前头几个测出真灵根的，方才还挺着胸脯，这时候胸脯不知怎么，慢慢瘪了下去。马小宝排在她后头隔一个，一口桂花糕嚼到一半忘了嚼，鼓在腮帮子里，好半天才咽下去，噎得直伸脖子。他扭过头去找他表伯，他表伯没看他，正低着头，拿袖子擦那支笔，擦了一遍又一遍。一百来双眼睛落在那个红鼻头的丫头身上，那眼神，同早上码头上的人看那锭银子，一模一样。

阿禾的脸给那片青照得发绿。她仰起头，看了看按在自己头顶上的那只手，又看了看那张和气的脸，想了一想，开了口。这是她进这座殿以后的头一句话：

「拜师……要交钱么？」

满殿的人一齐愣住，好几张嘴张着，半天合不上。玄沉子也愣了一愣，那只手没有拿开，一张和气的脸上，慢慢露出一点笑来：「不交。」阿禾点点头。玄沉子回到蒲团上坐下，她便站在蒲团边上，两只手攥着那个蓝布面的本子，往观主身后缩了半步。那一片青，这时候才一点一点退回石头里去。

小满排在她后头三个，看得清清楚楚。他想喊。一个「禾」字已经从嗓子眼里冲上来，冲到牙齿后头，停住了——满殿的人都在看她，执事在看殿门外头。这一嗓子喊出去，是告诉满殿的人：这个丫头有人认得，是石坳村的，她家住哪儿，她爹叫什么。他张了嘴，到底没喊出声来，把那个字咽了回去，咽得喉咙生疼。

去年冬天，那个穿白的进过石坳村两回，两回都站在沈家院子里。隔一道篱笆，就是老周家。他没往那边看过一眼——他找的是狐狸。

轮到马小宝了。执事看了一眼名册，道：「一百零七。还剩一个。」马小宝把手往测灵石上一拍，拍得「啪」的一声，好像拍的是自家的桌子。测灵石亮了，金白、红、黄三种颜色，却发浑，像蒙了一层灰。执事念道：「金、火、土，三灵根，色浊。中下之资。」他伸手要过马小宝的考牌，一看，一道，一个圈，还空着一格，眉头便皱了起来。马小宝身后那个家丁凑上前，把那封荐书又亮了一亮。执事看看荐书上的落款——那落款，他是认得的，是侧座上那位崔长老的私印——又看看观主。观主没有说话。蒲团上那位圆脸的崔长老，眼皮也没抬，慢悠悠吹了吹茶沫，道：「荐书是老夫写的。这孩子，记在我名下。」执事便提起笔来，在那空着的一格里，自己添了一道，道：「长老的荐书在，这一格，算补过了。」又在名册上写了个字，把最后那一格划掉了：「一百零八。名额满了。后头的，不用测了。」

后头只剩小满一个。他没有走。他在心里算：不测，考牌上三道，就是三道白画；测了，就算不取，名册上也有他沈小满一行。他道：「执事，我三道画满了。我测。」执事看了看他手里的考牌，拿下巴一指：「测吧。测完了下山。」

他往前走的时候，心里那块石头又压了上来——不是名额，是眼前这块测灵石。它测的是人身上的灵气；那他胸口木牌里睡着的那个，算不算他身上的？「藏。在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王。」小满的手心里，登时出了一层冷汗。他隔着衣裳，把那块木牌往怀里按了按。

他把手放在测灵石上。
story.en:
The main hall stood on the highest terrace inside the gate. It was large and old, the paintings on its beams faded to shadows; there was no statue in it, only, in the very middle, an empty stone stand. The stand was square, four feet beneath, big enough for a man to lie on, and in the middle of its top was a patch darker than the rest, square, as if many years ago something very, very heavy had once pressed there. In front of it stood a spirit-testing stone taller than a man, dusty grey, nothing remarkable to look at. On a cushion beside the stand sat the abbot — the man from the turtle's back that morning. A grey robe, a mild face, looking even kinder than a cloth merchant in the town below; yet of the hundred-odd children in the hall, not one dared lift his head to look at him twice. The old sweeper had come into the hall too, no one knew when, leaning on his broom in the doorway.

The children who had passed all three trials, a hundred or so in all, lined up in a long queue in the hall. Xiaoman was last, with only Ma Xiaobao, carried up in his chair, behind him. Calling the names was the same steward who had called them that morning at the foot of the stair, the face that had never quite woken up, leaning against a pillar.

A child asked what the stone stand was for and why it held no god; the roll-calling steward said, "Kept for a *ding*. Three hundred years now."

The steward pointed his chin at the testing stone, yawned, and recited the rules as usual — once every three years, droned like a sutra: "Hand on it. Metal white-gold, wood green, water black, fire red, earth yellow — whatever's in you, that's what lights. One colour: a single root, also called a heavenly root — highest of the high." Another yawn. "Don't bother looking. This temple hasn't tested one in three hundred years. Heavenly-root babies get carried off in swaddling clothes by the great sects, for silver; they never get as far as climbing these stairs. Outside the gate, others pick first. Whatever's left and comes through the gate belongs to this temple." A child asked: "A baby in swaddling clothes can't even talk — how can anyone tell?" The steward didn't lift his eyelids. "It's written in the *Baopuzi*: 'All who attain immortality met the breath of the immortals at the moment their fate was given — it is what they were born with. So even in the womb they already carry a nature that leads to the Way.' Born with it; the stone only shows it."

No one in the hall laughed at that. Xiaoman looked at the face that had never quite woken. He thought of that sheet of green on the landing, of that cry, "Brother —". Born with it; a stone shows it; silver is set down, and the child is carried off. So this was the rule, and the rule was written in a book.

The steward went on, faster and faster: "Two, a double root, above the middle; three, a triple root, just above the middle — both count as true roots. Four or five, false roots: four, below the middle; all five lit —" he drew it out, lifting his eyelids to run his gaze down the line, "— the lowest of the low. Fewer colours, brighter, better. No colour at all but a gust, a flash, a skin of frost — a variant root; this temple's never seen one, so don't get ideas. This year the outer court takes a hundred and eight. Abbot Xuanchenzi nods, you're in." Brush in hand, he counted down the register one by one, a stroke for each taken. Halfway down, the brush slid over one line without stopping; under that line were four freshly written words.

The queue crept forward inch by inch. Each time the stone lit up front, the hall made a noise — the light didn't sit on the surface; it rose layer by layer from inside the stone, and each time it did the whole hall turned a shade cooler, as if rain had just fallen — a bright one, a gasp; a dim one, a laugh. The barefoot boy from last night's veranda was ahead in the line, grass leaves still under his soles; he pressed, and four colours lit — "below the middle". He grinned and held up one finger to the crowd behind him. The steward asked his birth date as usual; he blurted out a year — at the foot of the stair he'd said twelve — and as soon as it was out his face went white. The steward counted on his fingers. "Eleven. The notice says twelve and up." The boy said, "Twelve after New Year!" The steward said, "After New Year, and three years after that, the next time the gate opens — come back then." The abbot looked at him a while, and didn't nod. The boy didn't cry. He went and stood in a corner of the hall, gripping his tag with its three full strokes.

Xiaoman counted as he shuffled: thirty-one people ahead, thirty-two places left in the register — enough; counting himself, just enough. When the ones ahead were down to twenty, there was a shove from behind, and the Ma servants squeezed Ma Xiaobao in ahead of him. Xiaoman counted again: twenty-one ahead, twenty-one places. He himself was the twenty-second. Sun Ergou, not far ahead, turned and grinned at him. "Three steps, one breath," he whispered. In the second trial he'd put the five in the middle "because five is right in the middle of one to nine, same as you put the rice bowl right in the middle of the table"; the old steward listened a long while, said the reasoning was wrong but the idea was right, and gave him a stroke. In the third he'd charged in with his eyes shut, run head first into the pine, raised a lump, and that counted as touching it.

Sun Ergou's turn. He laid his hand on it, and for a long while the stone did nothing; then, very grudgingly, a little light seeped out, four colours, faint as if seen through window paper. The name-calling steward thought the stone had broken and slapped it twice; the light got no brighter. The steward sighed and read: "Metal, wood, fire, earth — four, a false root, and very faint besides. The lowest of the low." Someone in the hall laughed. Sun Ergou didn't laugh, and didn't lower his head either; he only hitched the bundle bigger than himself higher on his back. In it were three pairs of shoes his mother had sewn, each bigger than the last, for him to grow into year by year on the mountain. The abbot looked at him a while, and nodded. The steward made a stroke.

Third in line ahead of Xiaoman was Ahe. She flicked her two little braids back over her shoulders and stepped up to the stone, but didn't press it at once. First she looked down at her hand — the back of it cracked in line after line, from a whole autumn of guarding a cabbage — wiped it twice on her robe, and only then laid it on.

The stone lit. One colour only.

Green. At first just a speck deep inside the stone, like the first shoot pushing up through frozen ground on the first day of spring; then the speck swelled, filled the stone, swelled out of the stone and filled the hall. A green with no mud in it, nothing mixed in, clean, not a thread of any other colour — so bright the whole hall threw up their arms over their eyes, and it was still bright, it came in between their fingers until the backs of their eyelids were green. The coolness in the hall turned all at once into a different smell: fresh-turned earth, the sap of snapped grass, as if someone had planted an acre overnight in a hall that hadn't held a god for three hundred years.

Xiaoman had seen that green on the landing that morning. That had been a stone the size of an egg.

Not a sound in the hall. The steward who called the names still had his mouth half open — "in three hundred years this temple has never found one": he'd recited it not a stick of incense ago, it was still hanging on his lips, and this green slapped it straight back into his face. His sleepy eyes were truly awake now, awake and staring. But the first thing he did was not read it out. He turned his head and flicked a glance out of the hall door.

There was nothing outside the door but sunlight, and the old sweeper leaning on the frame. Xiaoman knew all the same whom he was glancing for: before dawn, on the landing, a man in white had carried off a child who lit green, and before he climbed into his carriage he had nodded to this man.

The steward opened his mouth. "Wood… wood —"

Before the word "heaven" could come out, the man on the cushion stood up. A hundred-odd children had been tested through most of the day and Xuanchenzi hadn't shifted once — bright, he nodded; dim, he nodded too, like a clay idol in a temple that knew how to nod. Now he stood, and came down from beside the stone stand, unhurried, the hem of his grey robe brushing the flagstones without a sound. He stopped before Ahe; the green hadn't faded yet, and it turned his mild face green too. He put out one hand and laid it on top of her head, between the two little yellow braids, and said:

"This one, I'm taking."

Then, following the steward's glance of a moment before, he looked out of the hall door, and said, not loudly, not as if to anyone in the hall:

"She is Chending Temple's."

On the doorframe, the old sweeper's broom came down on the threshold with a *tock*. The steward's brush hung over the register a long while before it would come down; at last he wrote two characters under her line: *personal disciple*. Smaller than he usually wrote. Then, as before, he struck one place off the count. Xiaoman counted again with him: he was still twenty-second.

Only then did the hall go off like a firecracker. Some counted the "three hundred years" on their fingers; some craned on tiptoe to see how many eyes the girl had; the few ahead who'd lit true roots had been puffing their chests out a moment ago, and now, somehow, their chests slowly went flat. Ma Xiaobao, one behind her in line, forgot to chew a mouthful of osmanthus cake halfway through; it sat bulging in his cheek a long while before he swallowed it and nearly choked, craning his neck. He turned to look for his uncle; his uncle didn't look at him — he had his head down, wiping that brush on his sleeve, over and over. A hundred-odd pairs of eyes rested on the red-nosed girl, and the look in them was the very look the landing had given that silver ingot that morning.

The green had turned Ahe's face green. She tipped her head back, looked at the hand on top of her head, then at the mild face, thought it over, and spoke. It was the first thing she'd said since she came into the hall:

"Becoming your disciple… does it cost money?"

The whole hall froze, a good many mouths hanging open and staying that way. Xuanchenzi stared too, for a moment; the hand stayed where it was, and a slow smile came over the mild face. "It doesn't." Ahe nodded. Xuanchenzi went back and sat down on his cushion, and she stood beside it, both hands clutching the blue-covered book, half a step back behind the abbot. Only then did the green ebb, little by little, back into the stone.

Xiaoman, three behind her, saw all of it. He wanted to shout. The word "He —" had already come up his throat as far as the back of his teeth, and stopped there. The whole hall was looking at her; the steward was looking out of the door. Shout now, and he'd be telling the whole hall: somebody knows this girl — she's from Shi'ao village, here's where she lives, here's her father's name. He opened his mouth, and didn't make a sound after all; he swallowed the word, and it hurt his throat going down.

Last winter the man in white had come to Shi'ao village twice, and both times he'd stood in the Shen family's yard. One fence over was Old Zhou's. He never looked that way once — he was looking for a fox.

Then it was Ma Xiaobao's turn. The steward looked at the register. "A hundred and seven. One left." Ma Xiaobao slapped his hand on the stone — *smack* — as if it were his own family's table. The stone lit: white-gold, red and yellow, but dingy, as if under a film of dust. The steward read: "Metal, fire, earth — three roots, muddy. Below the middle of the middle." He held out his hand for Ma Xiaobao's tag, looked — one stroke, one circle, one square still empty — and frowned. The servant behind Ma Xiaobao stepped up and showed the letter of recommendation once more. The steward looked at the signature on the letter — a signature he knew — then at the abbot. The abbot said nothing. So the steward took up his brush and added a stroke in the empty square himself. "The letter stands; this square counts as made up." Then he wrote a word in the register and struck out the last place. "A hundred and eight. Places full. The rest needn't be tested."

Only Xiaoman was left behind. He didn't go. He reckoned: not tested, three strokes on his tag were three strokes for nothing; tested, even if not taken, the register would have a line with Shen Xiaoman on it. He said: "Steward, my three strokes are full. I'll be tested." The steward looked at the tag in his hand and pointed his chin. "Go on then. Then go down the mountain."

As he stepped forward the stone in his heart pressed down again — not the places now, but this testing stone in front of him. It tested the spirit qi in a person; then the one asleep in the token on his chest — did she count as his? "Hide. Until you can beat everyone, no one is to know of me." A layer of cold sweat broke out on Xiaoman's palms. Through his clothes he pressed the token closer to his chest.

He laid his hand on the testing stone.

label.en: Give your birthday · The root test

exits.means: gives the day they were born, or lets the stone read them — the page card asks it

story.zh:
测灵石亮了——亮得很暗。

金白、青、黑、红、黄，五种颜色，一样不少，都有一点，哪一种都不多，哪一种都不亮，你挤着我，我挨着你，灰蒙蒙地搅在一处，像他娘拿家里用剩下的五种碎布头，拼成的一块抹布。{主亮}

殿里静了一静。

然后，有人笑出了声。笑得最响的，是马小宝。他笑得前仰后合，笑得手里的桂花糕渣子掉了一地，拿手指着那块测灵石，如同指着一个天大的笑话。他这一笑，殿里的孩子们便都笑了，一个传一个，一片一片地笑开去，笑声撞在那褪了色的大梁上，又落下来。

唱名的执事也笑了一笑，拖长了声音念道：「金、木、水、火、土——五行俱全。五门俱全的伪灵根，外门叫杂灵根。下下之资。」他提起笔来，「名额已满。不取。」

笔尖朝名册上「不取」那一栏落下去。小满站在测灵石跟前，手还放在石头上，没有拿下来。三百级是他自己走上来的，洛书是他自己算出来的，蠪侄的真头是他自己听出来的——到头来，一块石头，一支笔。他想起舅舅在一百六十级上坐下的那一炷香，想起林子口草地上那件盖着的破袄。满殿的人，笑的笑，看的看，只有两个人没有笑：一个是蒲团上的观主；另一个是阿禾。她站在观主的蒲团边上，低着头，拿炭条在本子上记了一笔，记得很重，炭条都记断了。

小满在心里飞快地算了一笔账：不说，是出去；说了，最多也是出去。他把手从测灵石上拿下来，从怀里摸出那块考牌，举了起来，道：「执事。」殿里的笑声小了一些。他道：「今天早上，石阶顶上那位老人家说，沉鼎观收人，不看出身，不看荐书，只看三样：腿，脑子，胆子。」他把考牌翻过来，让执事看那三道，「三样，我这牌子上画满了。」他顿了一顿，没有看马小宝，只道，「最后那个名额，牌子上一个圈，一道是执事自己添的。」

殿里一下子静了。静了一会儿，队伍前头，孙二狗一声不吭，也把自己的考牌举了起来。跟着，殿角那个光脚的孩子也举了起来——他是不取的，举得比谁都高，牌子上三道，是他一试一试爬出来的。举牌子的只有这两个，别人都低着头。

执事的脸涨成了猪肝色，笔尖一转，指着小满喝道：「放肆！名额的事，轮得到你一个杂灵根来说？来人——」

笔尖离名册还有一寸，观主开了口：「慢。」他看了看测灵石，又看了看小满。他看小满的时候，比看测灵石的时候长得多，长得小满都有点发毛了。然后他转过头去，问靠在殿门口的那个人：「三试。瞿老以为如何？」

殿里的孩子们这才知道，那扫地的老头，原来是有名字的。瞿老拄着扫帚，只说了四个字：「腿稳。心细。」殿柱边上的几个老执事，互相看了一眼。瞿老四十多年没有收过一个徒弟；这四十多年里，他评孩子的话，统共评过不到三回，每回不超过两个字。

玄沉子点了点头：「收。外门。」执事的笔停在半空，道：「观主，名额——」玄沉子道：「添一个。」

执事张了张嘴，到底没说出什么来，低下头，在名册的末尾添了一行，又在那一行后头，添了两个小字：顶撞。然后挨个收新弟子的考牌。收到小满跟前，门口的瞿老道：「留着。」执事的手缩了回去。马小宝从小满身边走过去的时候，瞿老拿扫帚把门槛扫了一下，扫得很响。马小宝压低了声音，拖长了腔：「沈——小——满。杂灵根，也进山门啊？」他咬了一口桂花糕，「山上的日子，长——着——呢。」小满也拖长了腔，一个字不差：「小宝哥，长——着——呢。」

那天夜里，有个起夜的老弟子路过正殿，看见观主一个人坐在那口空石座旁边的蒲团上，也不打坐，也不念经，看着那口石座，一直坐到了三更。
story.en:
The spirit-testing stone lit — very dimly.

White-gold, green, black, red, yellow — five colours, not one missing, a little of each, none much, none bright, jostling one another, stirred together grey and murky, like a rag his mother had stitched from five kinds of leftover scraps. {主亮}

The hall went still for a moment.

Then someone laughed out loud. Loudest of all was Ma Xiaobao. He laughed till he rocked, laughed cake crumbs all over the floor, pointing at the testing stone as if at the joke of the century. With him laughing, the children in the hall all laughed, one catching it from the next, spreading patch by patch, the laughter hitting the faded beams and falling back down.

The name-calling steward smiled too, and drew it out as he read: "Metal, wood, water, fire, earth — all five elements. A false root with all five gates — the outer court calls it a mixed root. The lowest of the low." He lifted his brush. "The places are full. Not taken."

The brush tip came down toward the "not taken" column of the register. Xiaoman stood before the testing stone, his hand still on it, not taking it away. The three hundred steps he had climbed himself, the Luo diagram he had reckoned himself, the Longzhi's true head he had heard himself — and at the end of it, a stone, and a brush. He thought of his uncle sitting down on the hundred-and-sixtieth step for the length of a stick of incense; he thought of the torn jacket laid over something on the grass at the forest's edge. Of all the hall, laughing or staring, only two did not laugh: one was the abbot on his cushion; the other was Ahe. She stood beside the abbot's cushion, head down, and made a mark in her book with her charcoal, so hard the charcoal snapped.

Xiaoman ran a quick sum in his head: say nothing, and he's out; speak, and at worst he's out. He took his hand off the testing stone, took the trial tag from his jacket, and held it up. "Steward." The laughter in the hall thinned. He said: "This morning, the old man at the top of the stair said Chending Temple takes disciples not by birth, not by letters of recommendation, but by three things only: legs, head, nerve." He turned the tag so the steward could see the three strokes. "Three things — my tag's full." He paused, didn't look at Ma Xiaobao, and said only: "The last place — its tag has a circle on it, and one stroke the steward drew himself."

The hall went silent at once. After a moment, near the front of the line, Sun Ergou, without a word, held up his own tag. Then the barefoot boy in the corner held his up too — he was the one not taken, and he held it higher than anyone, three strokes on it, climbed one trial at a time. Only those two raised their tags; everyone else kept their heads down.

The steward's face went liver-red; he swung the brush tip round at Xiaoman and barked: "Insolence! Are the places the business of a mixed root? Someone —"

The brush tip an inch from the register, the abbot spoke: "Wait." He looked at the testing stone, then at Xiaoman. He looked at Xiaoman much longer than at the stone, so long Xiaoman's skin began to prickle. Then he turned and asked the man leaning in the doorway: "The three trials. What does Elder Qu think?"

Only then did the children in the hall learn that the old sweeper had a name. Elder Qu leaned on his broom and said just four words: "Steady legs. Careful heart." A few old stewards by the pillars exchanged a look. Elder Qu had taken no disciple in over forty years; in those forty-odd years he had given a verdict on a child fewer than three times, never more than two words a time.

Xuanchenzi nodded. "Accepted. Outer court." The steward's brush hung in mid-air. "Abbot — the places —" Xuanchenzi said: "Add one."

The steward opened his mouth, said nothing in the end, lowered his head and added a line at the end of the register — and after that line, two small characters: *insubordinate*. Then he went along collecting the new disciples' trial tags. When he reached Xiaoman, Elder Qu in the doorway said: "Keep it." The steward's hand drew back. As Ma Xiaobao walked past Xiaoman, Elder Qu swept the threshold once with his broom, very loud. Ma Xiaobao lowered his voice and drew it out: "Shen — Xiao — man. A mixed root, through the gate, eh?" He bit into his osmanthus cake. "Days on this mountain are lo-o-ong." Xiaoman drew it out too, word for word: "Xiaobao-ge — lo-o-ong."

That night an old disciple, up in the night, passed the main hall and saw the abbot sitting alone on the cushion beside the empty stone stand, not meditating, not chanting, looking at the stand, until the third watch.
